questions.question: Which of the following is NOT explicitly listed as a core pillar of this course?
questions.explanation: The course focuses on solving, proving correctness, and arguing efficiency, not on mastering a specific language.
questions.flashcard_front: What are the three core pillars of this course?
questions.flashcard_back: Solving computational problems, proving correctness, and arguing efficiency.
questions.flashcard_explanation: These three pillars form the foundation of the course's approach to algorithms.

questions.question: The course emphasizes writing to explain and justify algorithmic solutions to others.
questions.explanation: The instructor explicitly states that students will do a lot of writing to communicate their ideas.
questions.flashcard_front: Is communication a key focus of this course?
questions.flashcard_back: Yes, it is essential for explaining and justifying solutions to others.
questions.flashcard_explanation: The course emphasizes communicating ideas to people, not just computers.

questions.question: Why does the instructor compare this course to a 'CI' (Communication Intensive) class?
questions.answer: Because students will be doing a lot more writing than they will be coding.
questions.explanation: The instructor notes that the course requires significant writing to communicate and prove algorithmic ideas.
questions.flashcard_front: Why is writing important in this course?
questions.flashcard_back: To prove correctness and communicate efficiency of solutions to others.
questions.flashcard_explanation: Writing is the primary tool for justifying and explaining algorithmic work.

questions.question: Beyond just solving a problem, what two things must you be able to do with your solution?
questions.explanation: The instructor highlights these as the two essential tasks beyond simply finding a solution.
questions.flashcard_front: What must you prove about your solution?
questions.flashcard_back: You must prove it is correct and argue its efficiency.
questions.flashcard_explanation: These are the two primary requirements for evaluating a computational solution.
